lessonInput.title: Relative dating rules
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Relative dating orders geological events by interpreting relationships such as superposition, inclusions, and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages. Claim 1: In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers. Claim 2: A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.
lessonInput.readings: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), section 8.2, BCcampus Open Education

claims: Relative dating orders geological events by interpreting relationships such as superposition, inclusions, and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages.
In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers.
A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.

anchors.quote: look at the relationships between them
the layers at the bottom are older than those at the top
must be younger than the feature that is disrupted

attribution: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), section 8.2, BCcampus Open Education

facts: Relative dating orders geological events by interpreting relationships such as superposition, inclusions, and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages.
In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers.
A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.

keyTerms.df: Relative dating is a way to place geological events in sequence by comparing how features relate to one another.
keyTerms.eg: A geologist orders two rock units by their relationship instead of a number.
keyTerms.mi: Relative dating gives each rock a numerical age.
keyTerms.cx: It compares event order from relationships and does not supply numerical ages.

keyTerms.df: Superposition is the rule for an undisturbed sedimentary sequence in which lower layers are older than layers above them.
keyTerms.eg: A lower sedimentary bed is matched with the older part of the stack.
keyTerms.mi: Superposition makes upper layers older in a layered sequence.
keyTerms.cx: The rule places older layers below younger layers in an undisturbed sequence.

keyTerms.df: Cross-cutting is a relationship in which a feature that cuts or disrupts another feature is placed later in time than the feature it affects.
keyTerms.eg: A fault that slices through a rock layer is younger than that layer.
keyTerms.mi: A cutting feature must be older than the rocks it crosses.
keyTerms.cx: A feature that disrupts another feature is younger than the feature disrupted.

scenario.su: A field team is mapping a cliff face where a narrow break slices through several sedimentary layers. They must decide whether the break formed before or after the layered sequence was deposited.
scenario.ma: The layered outcrop shows lower beds beneath higher beds, a narrow break that crosses multiple layers, and a note that the sequence is undisturbed; the cross-cutting trace and the bed order are the records to compare.

mc.q: In the roadcut, one thin vein slices across three layered beds, while the beds themselves remain stacked in place. Which statement best matches the relationship between the vein and the beds?
op: The vein is younger than the beds
The vein is older than the beds
The beds are younger than the vein
The vein and beds formed together
mc.ex: The cut across the beds is direct evidence that the vein formed after the beds it disrupts. The same observation does not support the idea that the vein is older than the rocks it crosses.

mc.q: A second outcrop shows a sedimentary stack that has not been disturbed, with the lowest bed under two higher beds. Which ordering fits that arrangement best?
op: Lowest bed is oldest here
Highest bed is oldest here
All beds are same age
Middle bed is oldest here
mc.ex: The undisturbed stack matches superposition, which places older layers below younger layers. The highest-bed choice reverses that vertical order.

facts: Relative dating orders geological events by interpreting relationships such as superposition, inclusions, and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages.
In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers.
A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.

keyTerms.df: Superposition is the principle that in an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, older layers are situated beneath younger layers.
keyTerms.eg: Observing a layer of sandstone resting directly on top of a layer of shale.
keyTerms.mi: Superposition means all layers are the same age and stacked randomly.
keyTerms.cx: Superposition specifically dictates that older layers must be below younger ones in an undisturbed sequence.

keyTerms.df: Cross-cutting describes a geological feature that cuts across or disrupts another existing geological feature.
keyTerms.eg: A fault line that cuts through a layer of limestone.
keyTerms.mi: Cross-cutting only applies to features that are the same age as the layer they cut.
keyTerms.cx: Cross-cutting implies the feature that cuts must be younger than the feature it disrupts.

keyTerms.df: Inclusions are features found within another geological feature that provide evidence of relative age.
keyTerms.eg: Finding fragments of igneous rock embedded inside a sedimentary rock layer.
keyTerms.mi: Inclusions only indicate that the two features were formed at the exact same time.
keyTerms.cx: Inclusions provide evidence of relative age by showing one feature is contained within another.

scenario.su: A geologist is examining a rock outcrop where a layer of sandstone is clearly resting on top of a layer of shale. The constraint is that the sequence must be undisturbed for the relative dating rules to apply.
scenario.ma: Compare the observation of the sandstone resting on the shale to a scenario where a dike cuts through the sandstone layer.

mc.q: When observing a sedimentary sequence, what relationship between layers is established by the principle of superposition?
op: Younger layers are always found below older layers.
Older layers are always found above younger layers.
Older layers are always found below younger layers.
Layers are stacked randomly without age correlation.
mc.ex: In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers, which supports the correct option.

mc.q: A feature is observed cutting across a layer of shale; what does this observation imply about the relative ages of the features?
op: The feature cutting the shale is older than the shale.
The feature cutting the shale is younger than the shale.
The feature cutting the shale is the same age as the shale.
The feature cutting the shale must be below the shale.
mc.ex: A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts, supporting the second option.

lessonInput.title: Magnetic force
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field. Claim 1: The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field. Claim 2: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

claims: Magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

anchors.quote: force on a moving charge in a magnetic field
perpendicular to the velocity and magnetic field
zero when velocity is parallel to the field

facts: Magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

keyTerms.df: Magnetic force is the interaction on a moving charge that varies with charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.
keyTerms.eg: A charge crossing a magnetic field can have a magnetic force that changes when its velocity direction changes.
keyTerms.mi: Magnetic force points along the velocity of the charge.
keyTerms.cx: The force is not along the velocity; it is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.

keyTerms.df: A moving charge is a charged object with velocity, so its magnetic force depends on that velocity and its direction relative to the magnetic field.
keyTerms.eg: A moving charge with velocity parallel to the field is a case with no magnetic force.
keyTerms.mi: Any charge must feel magnetic force whether it is moving or not.
keyTerms.cx: The dependence is on a moving charge, so the velocity and its angle to the field matter.

keyTerms.df: A magnetic field is the field in this relation that sets the direction and orientation used to determine the magnetic force on a moving charge.
keyTerms.eg: A magnetic field compared with a charge's velocity helps determine whether the force is present and how it is oriented.
keyTerms.mi: A magnetic field can only be compared by its strength, not by its direction.
keyTerms.cx: Direction matters because the force depends on the angle between velocity and field and is perpendicular to both.

scenario.su: A student records a charge moving through a magnetic field and needs to decide whether the magnetic force is present. The lab note says the velocity is parallel to the magnetic field, and the setup must be judged before the next run.
scenario.ma: Notebook entry: velocity parallel to magnetic field; diagram sketch: arrows drawn in the same direction; observation log: no magnetic force marker; comparison card: a perpendicular setup shown beside the parallel setup.

mc.q: A lab sketch shows a moving charge with its velocity drawn at right angles to the magnetic field. Which statement matches the magnetic force and magnetic field relation?
op: Force follows the velocity direction
Force depends on angle only
Force aligns with the magnetic field
Force is perpendicular to both vectors
mc.ex: The force depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and angle, and it is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field. The closest distractor reverses the direction relation by making the force follow the velocity.

mc.q: In a test run, the charge moves parallel to the magnetic field line marked on the diagram. Which interpretation fits the observation and the recorded setup?
op: Force depends on charge only
No magnetic force is experienced
Force points with the velocity
Force is perpendicular to field
mc.ex: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force. The closest distractor uses the perpendicular relation, but that relation does not apply to the parallel setup.

facts: Magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

keyTerms.df: The magnetic force on a moving charge is determined by the charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between them.
keyTerms.eg: Calculating the force on an electron moving at a specific speed through a known magnetic field.
keyTerms.mi: The magnetic force is only dependent on the charge and the magnetic field strength.
keyTerms.cx: The magnetic force also depends on the velocity and the angle between the velocity and the magnetic field.

keyTerms.df: Velocity is a factor in determining the magnetic force on a charge, as it is one of the variables considered.
keyTerms.eg: Determining the magnetic force when a charge moves at a high speed through a magnetic field.
keyTerms.mi: Velocity does not affect the magnetic force calculation at all.
keyTerms.cx: Velocity is a necessary component in determining the magnetic force on a moving charge.

keyTerms.df: The magnetic field is a physical quantity that influences the magnetic force experienced by a moving charge.
keyTerms.eg: Analyzing how a charge interacts with a uniform magnetic field in a circuit.
keyTerms.mi: A magnetic field only affects charges that are stationary.
keyTerms.cx: A magnetic field influences the magnetic force on a moving charge, regardless of whether the charge is stationary or moving.

scenario.su: A test charge moves with a velocity of $v$ through a uniform magnetic field $B$. The charge has a positive value, and the angle between the velocity and the magnetic field is $0$ degrees. Determine the resulting magnetic force on the charge.
scenario.ma: Compare the magnetic force calculated when the charge moves at an angle of $30$ degrees to the field versus when the charge moves parallel to the field, noting the resulting force in both cases.

mc.q: When a charge moves parallel to a magnetic field, what is the resulting magnetic force on the charge?
op: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and magnetic field.
The magnetic force depends on the charge, velocity, magnetic field, and angle.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.
The magnetic force is determined by the charge and the magnetic field strength.
mc.ex: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force, which is supported by the fact that a charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

mc.q: If a charge moves at an angle of $30$ degrees to a magnetic field, which statement accurately describes the relationship between the velocity and the magnetic field?
op: The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
The magnetic force is determined by the charge and the magnetic field strength.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.
The magnetic force depends on the charge, velocity, magnetic field, and angle.
mc.ex: The magnetic force depends on the charge, velocity, magnetic field, and angle, which is supported by the fact that magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.

lessonInput.title: Capital accumulation
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: The capital stock is the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production; it rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation. Claim 1: Net investment, which is gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period. Claim 2: The capital stock grows only when net investment is positive.

claims: The capital stock is the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production; it rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation.
Net investment, which is gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.
The capital stock grows only when net investment is positive.

anchors.quote: rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation
gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period
the stock grows only when net investment is positive

facts: The capital stock is the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production; it rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation.
Net investment, which is gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.
The capital stock grows only when net investment is positive.

keyTerms.df: The capital stock is the production-side collection of equipment, structures, and tools described by the ledger.
keyTerms.eg: An inventory of equipment, structures, and tools is the capital stock in this context.
keyTerms.mi: The capital stock means only money held for production decisions.
keyTerms.cx: That reading fails because the ledger defines it as equipment, structures, and tools available for production.

keyTerms.df: Gross investment is the addition-side flow paired with depreciation when describing how the capital stock changes.
keyTerms.eg: A record showing gross investment beside depreciation uses the term in the ledger's setup.
keyTerms.mi: Gross investment is the same thing as the net change in capital stock.
keyTerms.cx: That is incorrect because the ledger separates gross investment from net investment and defines the latter as the change.

keyTerms.df: Net investment is the difference between gross investment and depreciation, and it tracks the change in capital stock over a period.
keyTerms.eg: A worksheet that subtracts depreciation from gross investment is using net investment exactly as stated.
keyTerms.mi: Net investment is simply another name for gross investment.
keyTerms.cx: That does not fit because the ledger defines net investment as gross investment minus depreciation.

scenario.su: A production manager reviews a sheet listing equipment, structures, and tools for production, plus separate lines for gross investment and depreciation. The manager must decide whether the capital stock can be said to grow in the period while keeping the record consistent.
scenario.ma: Compare the equipment, structures, and tools entry, the gross investment line, and the depreciation line; then compare the net investment notation with the statement that growth occurs only when net investment is positive.

mc.q: A record lists gross investment and depreciation beside a change statement. Which relation matches the listed terms when the change is computed from the two flow entries?
op: Gross investment equals capital stock minus depreciation.
Capital stock equals gross investment minus depreciation.
Net investment equals gross investment minus depreciation.
Depreciation equals gross investment minus net investment.
mc.ex: The ledger says net investment is gross investment minus depreciation, and that is the change in capital stock over a period. The tempting reversal treats capital stock as if it were the subtraction result, but that relation is not what the ledger states.

mc.q: A worksheet shows gross investment of 18 and depreciation of 11 for the period. Based on the recorded relation, which statement about the capital stock is supported?
op: The capital stock stays fixed because depreciation is present.
The capital stock grows because net investment is positive.
The capital stock grows because gross investment is positive.
The capital stock falls because gross investment is positive.
mc.ex: Gross investment exceeds depreciation here, so net investment is positive, and the capital stock grows. The closest distractor mistakes gross investment for the condition that alone determines growth, but the ledger ties growth to positive net investment.

facts: The capital stock is the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production; it rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation.
Net investment, which is gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.
The capital stock grows only when net investment is positive.

keyTerms.df: The total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production.
keyTerms.eg: A factory's machinery and buildings constitute the capital stock.
keyTerms.mi: Capital stock is only the new equipment purchased during a period.
keyTerms.cx: Capital stock is the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production.

keyTerms.df: The component of capital stock growth that increases the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools.
keyTerms.eg: Purchasing new machinery is an example of gross investment.
keyTerms.mi: Gross investment is the total change in the capital stock over time.
keyTerms.cx: Gross investment is the component that causes the capital stock to rise.

keyTerms.df: The change in the capital stock over a period, calculated by subtracting depreciation from gross investment.
keyTerms.eg: If gross investment exceeds depreciation, net investment is positive.
keyTerms.mi: Net investment is simply the gross investment without any accounting for wear and tear.
keyTerms.cx: Net investment is the change in the capital stock over a period, calculated by subtracting depreciation from gross investment.

scenario.su: A manufacturing firm observes that its total capital stock increased by $5 million this year. The firm's gross investment was $6 million, and depreciation was $1 million. The constraint is that the firm must maintain a positive capital stock growth rate to satisfy regulatory requirements.
scenario.ma: Compare the capital stock change calculated using gross investment and depreciation against the change calculated using net investment.

mc.q: If gross investment is $6 million and depreciation is $1 million, what is the resulting change in the capital stock over the period?
op: The change is $6 million plus $1 million.
The change is $6 million minus $1 million.
The change is $5 million plus $1 million.
The change is $6 million minus $5 million.
mc.ex: Net investment, which is gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period. The change is $6 million minus $1 million, which is $5 million, correcting the option suggesting addition of depreciation.

mc.q: A firm's capital stock is currently $100 million, and its gross investment is $10 million while depreciation is $2 million; what is the status of the capital stock growth?
op: The capital stock grows because gross investment is positive.
The capital stock grows because net investment is positive.
The capital stock grows because depreciation is less than gross investment.
The capital stock grows because the capital stock is currently large.
mc.ex: The capital stock grows only when net investment is positive. Since net investment is $10 million minus $2 million, which is $8 million, the capital stock grows because net investment is positive, correcting the option suggesting gross investment alone determines growth.

lessonInput.title: Sensory receptors and perception
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Sensory receptors detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals; perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns. Claim 1: Receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations. Claim 2: Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.

claims: Sensory receptors detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals; perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.
Receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations.
Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.

anchors.quote: Perception is the central processing of sensory stimuli into a meaningful pattern
Receptors are the cells or structures that detect sensations
Stimuli from varying sources, and of different types, are received and changed into the electrochemical signals of the nervous system

facts: Sensory receptors detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals; perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.
Receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations.
Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.

keyTerms.df: Sensory receptors are structures or cells that detect stimuli and pass them into nervous-system signaling.
keyTerms.eg: A handout labels a skin sensor as a sensory receptor when it detects a touch stimulus.
keyTerms.mi: A student thinks sensory receptors are the same thing as the meaning made from signals.
keyTerms.cx: That is not correct because sensory receptors detect stimuli, while perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.

keyTerms.df: Perception is the central processing step that organizes nervous-system signals into meaningful patterns.
keyTerms.eg: A worksheet note says the brain step that makes patterns from signals is perception.
keyTerms.mi: A student thinks perception is the structure that detects sensations at the body surface.
keyTerms.cx: That is not correct because perception is processing of signals, while receptors are the cells or structures that detect sensations.

keyTerms.df: Electrochemical signals are the nervous-system signals produced when stimuli are changed into a signal form.
keyTerms.eg: A margin note says stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals before later processing.
keyTerms.mi: A student thinks electrochemical signals are the original stimuli arriving unchanged.
keyTerms.cx: That is not correct because the ledger says stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.

scenario.su: A student is sorting two notebook passages before a short check-in on body signaling. One passage says a structure detects a stimulus, and the other says signals are processed into meaningful patterns.
scenario.ma: Passage A: "detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals"; Passage B: "central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns".

mc.q: A diagram points to a body structure that detects touch, while a margin note describes the nervous system making meaning from signals. Which pairing matches sensory receptors and perception?
op: Detection by receptors, processing by perception
Processing by receptors, detection by perception
Signals become receptors, stimuli become perception
Meaning-making by receptors, sensation by perception
mc.ex: The ledger says sensory receptors detect stimuli, and perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns. The closest distractor swaps those roles, but processing belongs to perception, not receptors.

mc.q: A worksheet shows one line saying sensations are detected by cells or structures, and another saying stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals. Which line should be classified as the signal-conversion step?
op: Stimuli changed into electrochemical signals
Cells or structures detect sensations
Meaningful patterns from nervous-system signals
Internal or external stimuli detected by receptors
mc.ex: The ledger explicitly states that stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system. The closest distractor names receptor detection, which is a different ledger relation from signal conversion.

facts: Sensory receptors detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals; perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.
Receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations.
Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.

keyTerms.df: Sensory receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations.
keyTerms.eg: A receptor detects a specific external stimulus like heat.
keyTerms.mi: Sensory receptors are the central processing of signals into patterns.
keyTerms.cx: Sensory receptors are the cells or structures that detect sensations, not the central processing of signals.

keyTerms.df: Perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.
keyTerms.eg: Perception processes signals into a meaningful pattern of pain.
keyTerms.mi: Perception is the cells or structures that detect sensations.
keyTerms.cx: Perception is the central processing of signals into patterns, not the cells that detect sensations.

keyTerms.df: Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.
keyTerms.eg: A stimulus causes a change into an electrochemical signal.
keyTerms.mi: Stimuli are cells or structures that detect sensations.
keyTerms.cx: Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system, not cells or structures that detect sensations.

scenario.su: A patient reports feeling a sharp sensation when touching a hot surface, and a technician observes a specific nerve ending responding to the heat. The constraint is that the student must distinguish between the initial detection and the subsequent processing of this sensation.
scenario.ma: Compare the observation of the nerve ending responding to heat with the definition of perception as the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.

mc.q: When a sensory receptor detects a stimulus, what is the immediate result according to the supplied claims?
op: Receptors convert stimuli into meaningful patterns.
Receptors detect sensations.
Stimuli become electrochemical signals.
Perception processes internal signals into patterns.
mc.ex: Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system, then receptors detect sensations, which is the correct sequence.

mc.q: A student observes that a specific cell detects a sensation, but fails to understand the role of the nervous system in signal conversion. Which statement best describes the relationship between receptors and signals?
op: Receptors are the central processing of signals into patterns.
Receptors detect sensations and convert stimuli into signals.
Stimuli are changed into receptors that detect sensations.
Perception is the cells that detect sensations.
mc.ex: Receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations, and stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system, which is the correct relationship.
